c6_free_family.title: The long table
c6_free_family.text: Your cousin pushes the pie across the table and looks at her plate. “I should have said it differently, that day.” “Yes,” you say. Then you pass the bread, and that is how it is mended.

c6_free_quill.title: Quill counts
c6_free_quill.text: Quill counts every basket twice. “A tenth,” he says, and writes it with a small flourish. “The Lord will like the numbers. I like them better.” He looks at your fields as if they were a poem.

c6_free_greenstem.title: Two healers
c6_free_greenstem.text: Greenstem takes the chest in both arms. “Wren says I may carry it to the village myself.” Wren, behind him, folds her arms and does not say a word. Her eyes say a lot.

c6_free_miller.title: The sails turn
c6_free_miller.text: The miller pours your flour into his hopper. The sails creak, then turn, slowly, as they did before the fire. “Hear that?” he says. “That is Hazelwood having bread again.”

c6_free_lark.title: Nutmeg
c6_free_lark.text: Lark holds out the cake. The squirrel takes it with both hands. “Nutmeg,” Lark announces. “Obviously.” The squirrel does not look as if it has any other opinion. You laugh until the fence shakes.

c6_free_garden.title: For the night garden
c6_free_garden.text: You set the bowl down at the edge of the garden. You open your mouth. You close it again. Far off, very softly, a very small bell rings twice. You nod, and walk home in the dark, and you are not afraid.

c6_lord.title: The Lord's letter
c6_lord.text: A rider brings a letter with a red seal. Your farm prospers, it says, so the share goes back to a half, “as before.” You read it twice. Inside you, an old pattern sits up and stretches.

c6_broker.title: The Import Broker
c6_broker.text: A new trader unpacks his cart on the square. He has a hat, a tune and a very familiar face. “Barter?” he says. “Yes!” He winks. You decide to stop wondering who he looks like.

c6_garden.title: White flowers at dusk
c6_garden.text: Where the marsh was, white flowers open at dusk. Hundreds of them, glowing softly. Somewhere in the dark, very quietly, bells. Nobody comes out to meet you. You stand there a long time and do not say a word.

c6_fair_letter.title: We're coming to the Fair
c6_fair_letter.text: A last letter from the river barge: “We're coming to the Fair. All of us. Even your cousin.” You put it in your pocket and keep touching it all day.

c6_fair_tables.title: The tables fill
c6_fair_tables.text: The tables at the Fair fill up. Everybody brought something: Pieter a lantern cake, Greenstem a basket of mint, the miller, with a face like thunder, a sack of flour. The whole village works with you.

c6_crisis.title: At the Fair
c6_crisis.text: The Fair is bright and loud. Then your cousin stands up in front of everyone. “You were in the barn that night,” she says. “I saw you run out, crying about lights.” The whole square goes quiet.

pages.text: You want to run. Instead you sit down on the nearest bench. Your hands are cold. Then you tell it: the lights in the dark, the lantern on the hook, the running, the shouting that nobody believed.
It is very quiet. Then your cousin sits down beside you. “I saw the lights too,” she says. “Nobody believed me either.” Somebody passes you a cup. Somebody passes her one, too.

c6_quill_answer.title: The Lord's answer
c6_quill_answer.text: Quill rides up with a new paper and, for the first time, a small smile. “With my numbers in hand, the Lord sets the share at a tenth, as in the old days.” He tips his hat. “They were very good numbers.”

pages.text: An alpaca stands at the gate, very tall and very polite. She lifts her head and hums one long, strange note, the note that woke the whole farm that night. Nobody was hurt because of her.
She spits, politely, on principle. The last line of the rhyme comes back, whole: “Soft alpaca guards all things.” You say all of it, from the very first line. Your voice does not wobble.
The long table, the lanterns, the whole village. You sit down at last, and nobody needs you to stand. You set a place for Lark without a word. He has to sit very still for a moment.
The goat eats the blue ribbon. Somebody starts to sing. You know the tune. You sing it, too.

c6_ajar.title: The edge of the night garden
c6_ajar.text: That night you walk to the edge of the dark garden. You came to say something. You stand there a long time. Somewhere in the white flowers a tiny bell moves, and is still. You go home. It is not time yet.

pages.text: The grandchildren are asleep, all but Minena. “Tell me the imp was real,” she whispers. You tell her the truth, all of it, quietly, the way it happened.
“If you ever meet a little fellow with bells,” you say, “tell him I was never angry.” Minena nods, very seriously. That night she dreams of a melody, and in the morning she hums it.
